rows.subtype: Lost in a game or puzzle [Actor]
rows.description: A child works on a building set, forgetting food and time, with challenge matching skill; the joy of full absorption builds concentration.
A teenager practising guitar or cricket forgets the phone and feels calm and clear afterwards; flow comes when a task is hard enough to need attention but not so hard that it frustrates.
A child feeling upset remembers only bad things about the week and expects tomorrow to be bad too. Feelings pick what the mind recalls.

A teenager in a low mood reads neutral messages as rejection and recalls only failures. Judgment feels like fact, though the mood is shaping it. Persistent low mood deserves caring adult attention and professional help.
A young adult in a great mood underestimates risks and says yes to too much. Joy, like sadness, tilts the thoughts that come to mind.
Spontaneously picking up dropped items or assisting others without explicit prompt or reward.
Aligning energy with social causes, volunteerism, and standing up for marginalized peers.
Structuring long-term career, family, and social choices around sustained societal contribution.
A preschooler hears a soft voice as safe and a harsh voice as anger or danger, even when the words are neutral. Children need help learning that a loud harsh voice is not always about them.
A listener hearing a trembling voice from a colleague or student may assume fear, grief, anger or excitement. The wise reading is to wait, stay warm and ask, rather than assume weakness or deception.

rows.subtype: Harsh voice at work and de-escalation [Interpreting]
rows.description: A young professional facing a harsh, raspy or strained voice from an angry client should treat it as a sign of high arousal. Lowering own volume, slowing down and acknowledging the concern usually calms the exchange.

rows.subtype: It will not happen to me [Actor]
rows.description: A child is sure he will not get caught, fall from the tree or fail the test. Bad outcomes seem to happen to other people.
A teenager riding without a helmet or vaping believes the harm is for others. Feeling invulnerable is partly developmental, since the brain weighs immediate reward heavily.
A graduate expects the first job, savings and relationship to go better than average and skips backup plans. Hope is healthy but unprepared hope is fragile.
A toddler sucks a thumb, twirls hair or strokes a blanket when tired or worried. These movements settle the nervous system and are a typical comfort; they usually fade with age and need no shaming.

rows.subtype: Touching the face and neck under stress [Regulating]
rows.description: A teenager rubs the neck, touches the face or bites nails before a presentation or a tough talk. These self-touches often calm nerves but are not reliable signs of hidden thoughts; slow breathing helps more.

A young adult clicks a pen, bounces a leg or uses stimming movements to focus or calm. For many neurodivergent people, stimming is a valid form of regulation; others should not read it as rudeness or lack of attention.
